title: Women's Cricket's Golden Era: How the Game Has Been Transformed
summary: The women's game is bigger, better funded, and more widely watched than at any point in its history. We trace the journey that brought it here and ask what comes next.
content:
When England and Australia contested the first Women's Ashes series in 1934, the game that existed was barely visible outside the countries that played it. For decades, women's cricket existed at the margins — played seriously, competed fiercely, but funded minimally and watched by tiny audiences compared to the men's game.

That story has changed dramatically. The Women's T20 World Cup, the Women's Ashes, the introduction of professional domestic contracts in major cricketing nations — women's cricket in 2026 is a different sport, in the best possible sense. It is a sport in a golden era, and the trajectory suggests that era is still building.

The Professionalism Revolution

The most significant structural change has been the professionalisation of the women's game in leading cricket nations. Central contracts — which allow players to train full-time, to focus entirely on cricket rather than balancing it with separate employment — transformed the standard of play when they were introduced, and have continued to raise it as the contracts have expanded in number and value.

England, Australia, India, and New Zealand now field teams of full-time professional cricketers. The difference in fitness, in technical preparation, in mental conditioning that full-time professional sport provides is visible in the standard of play at the highest level. The women's game is simply better than it was ten years ago, in ways that are directly attributable to the resources invested.

Australia's Sustained Excellence

Southern Stars have dominated women's cricket with a consistency that the game's other nations have consistently struggled to match. Megs Lanning's captaincy era, and the players around her — batters of genuine international class, a bowling attack with variety and penetration, a fielding standard that embarrasses many men's teams — produced a team that won World Cups with something approaching inevitability.

The Australian women's programme is a template: invest early in girls' development, provide professional contracts that enable full-time commitment, build a domestic competition that prepares players for international cricket, and maintain coaching and medical support that reduces injury and maximises performance. Other nations have studied it. Some have implemented versions of it. The gap has closed, but Australian excellence remains the standard.

Women's cricket is not the future of the game. It is part of the present of the game. We are not asking for a seat at the table. We have earned it, and we intend to build on it. The sport is better for having us at its centre.

Smriti Mandhana and the Indian Effect

India's commercial power in cricket — the broadcasting revenues, the sponsorship values, the audience size — has begun to flow into women's cricket in ways that will transform the game's economics. The Women's Premier League, launched in 2023 with franchise teams and broadcast deals that generated genuine commercial interest, represents the beginning of a process that could do for women's cricket what the IPL did for the men's game.

Smriti Mandhana, India's most celebrated women's cricketer, brings the kind of visibility that creates fans rather than simply keeping existing ones. Her batting — elegant, attacking, capable of the full range of strokes — translates beautifully to highlight packages that reach audiences who had never previously engaged with women's cricket.

The Road Ahead

Broadcast deals are growing. Attendances at marquee women's matches are increasing. Sponsorship interest from companies that recognise the demographic value of women's sport audiences is rising. The fundamentals that drive commercial sports are, increasingly, working in women's cricket's favour. The game that was at the margins is now at the mainstream. The only question is how much further it can go.
